About

René Descartes famously said: "I think, therefore I am.
"I asked my C++ compiler the same question.
It responded: Error: 'I' was not declared in this scope.

That pretty much sums up how I approach engineering

I’m a Computer Science student focused on:

Compilers & IR design

Hardware-aware programming (HLS, RTL, system-level thinking)

Bridging software ↔ hardware abstraction gaps

Currently building:

KUTUKA : A specialized C++ to System Verilog transpiler engineered to generate deterministic, ultra-low-latency hardware architectures primarily for High-Frequency Trading (HFT) systems.

I care about:

Deterministic systems over black-box abstractions

Performance that can be reasoned about (not guessed)

Designs grounded in real constraints: latency, memory, and hardware

If you're working on compilers, low-level systems, or hardware-software co-design, we’ll get along.

  • Rohit Chauhan

    7mo

    Just benchmarked Kutuka against industry standards (Vitis HLS 2025.2 and Intel HLS 24.1) for compiling High-Frequency Trading (HFT) triggers from C++ to RTL.
    The result: A 17x reduction in latency.
    Traditional HLS tools are powerful for complex algorithm acceleration, but they heavily rely on pipelines, multi-cycle FSMs, and time-multiplexing to optimize for area. For ultra-low-latency combinatorial dataflow, this introduces unacceptable overhead.
    Here is the data from compiling the exact same C++ algorithm:
    Latency: Kutuka achieved 1 cycle (pure combinatorial). Vitis took 16 cycles. Intel required an estimated 12-15 cycles.
    Timing @ 500MHz: Kutuka's single-cycle datapath provides clean timing. Vitis HLS failed timing with a -0.48ns slack.
    RTL Complexity: Kutuka generated 3 clean, auditable SystemVerilog files. Vitis generated 19. Intel generated 65+ files of infrastructure overhead.
    By strictly prioritizing single-cycle combinatorial synthesis over area-first time-multiplexing, Kutuka allows developers to hit ultra-low-latency targets without abandoning C++ programmability.

    Question for the FPGA and HFT community: Have we become too reliant on pipelined HLS architectures, even when pure combinatorial speed is the actual requirement? I'd love to hear your thoughts.
    #FPGA #HLS #HighFrequencyTrading #SystemVerilog #HardwareDesign #Cplusplus

      A brief on a recent engineering project.
      My interest in hardware description languages started entirely by chance. While trying to pass time in college library, I picked up a book called "Verilog HDL guide 2nd edition " by Samir Palnitkar. Reading it sparked several questions about the existing gaps between high-level software abstractions and low-level hardware design. "why is the HLS domain still so non-deterministic compared to tools like LLVM or Clang? We have such granular control over the backend in software, yet HLS tools often feel like black boxes that introduce jitter where we need precision."
      I reached out to multiple industry experts like , "Chris Lattner","Mehdi Amini","Steve Casselman"and "dr . Uday Reddy Bondhugula" looking for answers or existing tools that solved this specific problem. When I couldn't find any satisfactory answers, I decided to build the solution myself.
      For sometime now , I have been developing Kutuka, a C++ to SystemVerilog transpiler.
      Recently, after completing a working Minimum Viable Product (MVP), I realized the underlying architecture was novel enough to protect. I have now filed a provisional patent application , Provisional Patent Application no. 202611023575 dated 27/02/2026, and the system is officially patent pending.
      To be clear, there is no incorporated startup or company right now—just a working MVP and a legally protected foundation. The immediate next step is to continue testing and refining the transpiler.
